transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Iran's Supreme Leader says this country will respond forcefully if anyone attacks it,
according to Iranian state media.
This comes as the U.S. and Israel say they're preparing for a potential return to hostilities
after the midterm elections next week.
Empirus Adil El-Shalchi has more.
Ayatollah Mushta Bachamane said that "any level or type of threat to Iran"
would face a "immediate and impactful response."
The Supreme Leader made the comments in a meeting with Iranian military officials,
according to Iranian state media.
He also ordered the military to update their attack plans with U.S. and Israeli targets.
This comes at a time when Iran has intensified its attacks on ships trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Iranian state media, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that on Friday,
four tankers, one of which was carrying two million barrels of oil,
caught fire after hitting mines in the strait.
Hadil El-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
The Justice Department's lawsuit to isolate certain ballots in the Alaska U.S. Senate election
over potential voter confusion, because two candidates have similar names,
continues with a new wrinkle.
Empirus Ryan Lucas has more.
The department wants the court to delay certification in the U.S. Senate race in Alaska.
If the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses by a small margin.
That's because there's another Dan Sullivan on the ballot,
and the argument is that having two people with the same name could confuse voters.
The state Supreme Court already ruled that both Sullivans could run.
Things seemed to have settled down until a New York Times report this week
that said Democrats recruited the second Dan Sullivan to run,
specifically to siphon votes away from the Republican.
The Justice Department revised its lawsuit to include those allegations.
Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation.
The Justice Department already has a criminal investigation underway.
Empirus Ryan Lucas reporting.
It's among a handful of races around the country expected to determine control of the Senate.
Virginia and D.C. are both suing to stop the Trump administration
from building a massive arch in the nation's capital.
Empirus Stephen Besaha reports veterans groups have also sued to stop the construction.
The Trump administration plans to break ground for the 250-foot arch near Arlington Cemetery
as early as November 5th, assuming approval by the National Capital Planning Commission.
But in a new court filing Saturday, Virginia and D.C. called the plan illegal
since the administration does not have approval from Congress
and that the arch would be nearly double the city's height limit.
A group of Vietnam War veterans have also sued,
saying the arch would disrupt the sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House.
President Trump has said he wants the arch both as a memorial
and a military complex to store drones and station snipers.
Stephen Besaha, NPR News, Birmingham, Alabama.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Top diplomats from the G20 are wrapping up two days of talks in Atlanta,
but they haven't come to an agreement on several critical issues,
including Russia's war in Ukraine and the Middle East.
The U.S. says it's focusing on energy and critical mineral supply chains.
As a result, the group representing the world's 20 biggest economies
won't issue a joint communique as they usually do,
but we'll have a chairman's statement summarizing the talks out this afternoon.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is there meeting with counterparts
from Australia, India, and Japan before leading today's final event.
Astronomers appear to have tracked down new X-ray sources
that are decidedly Halloween-themed.
Reporter Ari Daniel has more.
Studying X-rays offers a window into the dynamics of extreme cosmic phenomena.
Researchers looking back at data collected by NASA's Chandra telescope
were stunned to find 84 new sources of the very lowest energy X-rays
spread across half a dozen galaxies.
It's likely they're produced by systems involving something super dense,
like a black hole, that's stealing material off a nearby star.
Like a vampire, says University of Alabama astronomer Jimmy Irwin.
Instead of stealing blood, they're stealing material from a companion star.
Another possible source could be two black holes orbiting one another,
pulling matter off a star, a situation that yields a kind of donut-shaped void
called a zombie disk.
For NPR News, I'm Ari Daniel.
And I'm Janine Hurst, and you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
